sections.authorBiography: William Shakespeare was baptized in Stratford-upon-Avon on 26 April 1564, married Anne Hathaway in 1582 and had three children, Susanna and the twins Hamnet and Judith. By the early 1590s he was writing and acting in London; from 1594 he was a sharer in the Lord Chamberlain's Men, the company that built the Globe on the south bank of the Thames in 1599. He wrote or co-wrote about 38 plays, including histories of English kings and tragedies drawn from Roman history, and died in Stratford on 23 April 1616. His fellow actors collected his plays in the First Folio of 1623.
sections.historicalContext: Julius Caesar dates from 1599, the year the Globe opened; a Swiss traveller, Thomas Platter, recorded seeing a play about Caesar at a Thameside playhouse on 21 September 1599. Shakespeare's source was Plutarch's Lives of the Noble Grecians and Romans in Thomas North's English translation (1579), which he followed closely, sometimes almost word for word. The historical Caesar was stabbed in the Senate house on the Ides of March (15 March) 44 BCE by senators led by Brutus and Cassius; Antony and Octavius defeated them at Philippi in 42 BCE. For English audiences in 1599 the story had urgent echoes: Queen Elizabeth I was old, had no heir, and the question of who would rule next, and whether resisting a ruler could ever be justified, was dangerous to discuss openly.

publicationAndReception.publication: The play was first printed in the First Folio (1623), in an unusually clean text that is thought to come from a theatrical manuscript. It is the first of Shakespeare's Roman tragedies drawn from Plutarch, followed by Antony and Cleopatra and Coriolanus.
publicationAndReception.then: It was popular from the start: the poet Leonard Digges, in verses printed in 1640, recalled audiences "ravish'd" by the quarrel scene between Brutus and Cassius while other plays emptied the house. It remained in the repertory after the Restoration and was among the most performed Shakespeare plays in the eighteenth century.
publicationAndReception.now: The play is a school standard, partly because it has little sexual content and centres on rhetoric and politics. Productions often make it about modern power: Orson Welles's 1937 Mercury Theatre staging dressed Caesar as a fascist dictator; Joseph Mankiewicz's 1953 film starred Marlon Brando as Antony; the Public Theater's 2017 Shakespeare in the Park production, with a Caesar resembling a contemporary president, provoked national controversy and lost sponsors. Critics debate who the hero is, Caesar or Brutus, and whether the assassination is presented as justified.

sections.overview: Julius Caesar returns to Rome in triumph, and some senators fear he will make himself king. Cassius sets out to persuade the respected Brutus to join a conspiracy. The play follows what they decide, what happens on the Ides of March, and how words, especially the speeches at Caesar's funeral, change the course of Rome.

spoilerOverview.text: The conspirators stab Caesar in the Capitol. Brutus lets Antony speak at the funeral; Antony's oration turns the crowd, and the conspirators flee. Antony, Octavius and Lepidus draw up a death list. Brutus and Cassius quarrel and reconcile; Portia has killed herself; Caesar's ghost visits Brutus. At Philippi Cassius has himself killed after misreading a report, and Brutus runs on his own sword; Antony calls him "the noblest Roman of them all."

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “The fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars, / But in ourselves, that we are underlings” slowly and put it in my own words: Cassius's line, among the most quoted in Shakespeare: a claim that people, not fate, are responsible. Ask students to watch whether the play agrees. Next, craft. I notice that the turn on “but” sets two ideas against each other. The word “underlings” is the strongest in the line; it sharpens the picture more than a plainer word would. Then, effect. What does this suggest about life beyond the story? My answer: Julius Caesar returns to Rome in triumph, and some senators fear he will make himself king.

strategies.label: Wait time
strategies.howTo: Pause at least 3 seconds after asking (5 to 10 for DOK 3 and 4 questions) before calling on anyone, and pause again after a student answers so others can add on. Call on students at random, not only volunteers.

strategies.label: Think-pair-share
strategies.howTo: One minute of silent thinking or jotting, two minutes with a partner, then pairs report. Use it for every DOK 3 and 4 question so all students rehearse an answer.

strategies.label: Follow-up probes
strategies.howTo: Answer a response with a probe instead of a verdict: ask for the line that proves it, ask "why?" or "how do you know?", or ask another student to agree, extend or challenge.

strategies.label: Student-generated questions
strategies.howTo: Students write their own questions at each level (a recall, a "why/how" and a "should/what if" question), trade them, and answer a classmate's. The teacher picks one or two for the whole class.

strategies.label: Turn and talk
strategies.howTo: A 60-second partner check for literal questions, so every student says the answer aloud before one is called on.

strategies.label: Cold call with support
strategies.howTo: Call on a student by name after the wait time; if they are stuck, offer a choice of two answers or let them "phone a friend" and come back to them.

strategies.label: Socratic circle
strategies.howTo: Inner circle discusses for 5 minutes while the outer circle tracks evidence and questions; then swap.

strategies.label: Four corners / take a stand
strategies.howTo: Students move to Agree / Somewhat agree / Somewhat disagree / Disagree and must cite a line to defend the position; anyone may move after hearing evidence.

literal.label: Literal / recall
literal.scaffold: Sentence starter: “In this scene, … because the text says …”
literal.extension: Note how this detail is set up or echoed elsewhere in Julius Caesar.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

inferential.label: Inferential / analytical
inferential.scaffold: Sentence starter: “The text says …, which suggests … because …”
inferential.extension: Test your reading against one critical approach (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) and say what it adds.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

evaluative.label: Evaluative / synthesis / creative
evaluative.scaffold: Sentence starter: “I (dis)agree that … because …; someone might object that …, but …”
evaluative.extension: Situate your judgment in a critical conversation about Julius Caesar: whose reading does yours support or challenge?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

segments.activity: Students write to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Project the day's bell-ringer question (each lesson of Julius Caesar has its own). Students write silently for 5 minutes, then pair-share for 3. Call on one volunteer and one non-volunteer, and connect their answers to power, ambition and tyranny.

segments.activity: Five key words in context, with verified word histories.
segments.script: Introduce the day's words in the sentences where they appear in Julius Caesar. Read each sentence aloud, ask students to guess the meaning from context, then give the gloss and the word history. Students copy one word into their journal with their own sentence.

Give the 10-minute background talk from the day's lesson: what happens in this scene, the context a reader needs, and the literary elements to watch. Pause once to ask a check-for-understanding question.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud in the day's lesson.
segments.script: Read the anchor passage aloud twice. Model the three steps out loud: what the words say, what craft choice stands out and why, and what effect it has on the reader. The day's lesson gives the passage and a full written think-aloud.

segments.activity: Guided analysis of a second quotation; expected answers given.
segments.script: Display the second passage. Students annotate it in pairs using the same three steps; circulate, then take answers to the two guided questions and confirm them against the expected answers in the day's lesson.

segments.activity: Independent annotation and a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph (exemplar given).
segments.script: Students annotate the scene on their own (three marks with a margin note each) and write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph on the day's focus, then begin the writing prompt at their assigned rigor level.

segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions, with facilitation notes.
segments.script: Run a 10-minute discussion from the day's anchor question and tiered questions. Start with literal checks, move to inference, and end with one evaluative question that ties the scene to power, ambition and tyranny.

segments.activity: Scene quiz in the app and an exit ticket (answer given).
segments.script: Students take the scene quiz in the app, then answer the one-sentence exit ticket with a short quotation. Collect the tickets to plan the next lesson.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Restate the day's takeaway in one sentence, ask two students to name the line that best proves it, and preview the next reading in Julius Caesar.

wholeBookTest.note: One version per rigor level; the teacher's class level picks the version and student auto-adjust applies (student override, then class standard, then automatic). items/answerKey hold the multiple-choice part of the HS Sophomore version for older clients.

middleSchool.label: Scaffolded support
middleSchool.text: Supported track: write a five-paragraph essay explaining what Julius Caesar teaches about power, ambition and tyranny. Use at least three quotations from passages your teacher selects from different parts of the book.

hsFreshman.label: HS Freshman
hsFreshman.text: Write a multi-paragraph essay explaining how William Shakespeare develops power, ambition and tyranny in Julius Caesar. Use evidence from the beginning, middle and end of the book.

hsSophomore.label: HS Sophomore
hsSophomore.text: Write an argumentative essay analyzing how William Shakespeare develops power, ambition and tyranny across Julius Caesar. Trace the idea through at least three scenes and address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.label: HS Junior
hsJunior.text: Write an analytical essay on how the structure of Julius Caesar (its order, turns and ending) shapes the meaning of power, ambition and tyranny. Discuss at least one place where the book leaves the question open.

hsSenior.label: HS Senior
hsSenior.text: Write a sustained argument comparing two interpretations of power, ambition and tyranny in Julius Caesar. Weigh the evidence for each and defend the stronger reading in a mature, well-organized essay.

ap.label: AP
ap.text: Write a literary argument: develop a defensible thesis about how William Shakespeare's choices in Julius Caesar (a recurring element, structure and narration) shape a complex understanding of power, ambition and tyranny, weigh at least one competing reading, and sustain commentary on well-chosen evidence. Do not merely summarize.

collegeFreshman.label: College Freshman
collegeFreshman.text: Write a researched essay (4–6 pages) that places Julius Caesar's treatment of power, ambition and tyranny in its historical context, using at least two scholarly sources.

collegeSophomore.label: College Sophomore
collegeSophomore.text: Write a contextual essay (6–8 pages) on power, ambition and tyranny in Julius Caesar that reads the play against its genre and period and engages two published critics. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeJunior.label: College Junior
collegeJunior.text: Write a theoretically informed essay (8–10 pages) on power, ambition and tyranny in Julius Caesar. Name your critical method, apply it closely, and acknowledge its limits. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeSenior.label: College Senior
collegeSenior.text: Write a research paper (12–15 pages) with an original argument about power, ambition and tyranny in Julius Caesar, engaging at least four scholarly sources in Chicago style. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

graduate.label: Graduate / PhD
graduate.text: Write a seminar paper (15–20 pages) that intervenes in the critical conversation on power, ambition and tyranny in Julius Caesar, engaging the relevant scholarship and textual history. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

finalPaper.title: Julius Caesar: final paper (formal literary analysis)

prompts.text: Analyze how William Shakespeare develops power, ambition and tyranny across Julius Caesar. Trace the idea through at least three moments (beginning, middle and end) and argue what the ending finally suggests.
Choose one recurring symbol, image or motif in Julius Caesar and argue how its meaning changes over the play and why that change matters to honor and self-deception.
Analyze a central character's choices in Julius Caesar. Argue whether the play judges that character, and how its structure or point of view shapes your answer.

Two readers disagree about whether Julius Caesar finally endorses or criticizes its society's view of rhetoric and persuasion. Weigh both readings and argue for one, answering the strongest objection.
